results.summary: This design measures the frequency of an external signal by counting pulses over 100 ms periods and displays the result on a 128x32 SSD1306 OLED display using an emulated 7-segment format. It requires an external 1 MHz clock, a PMOD OLED display, and the signal to be measured connected to the input pin. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and uses SPI to communicate with the OLED. No silicon test results are provided, so the actual performance is not documented.

This is an analog voltage-controlled oscillator built from four differential stages with capacitive loading, providing eight output taps with phase differences. The frequency is controlled by a bias current or voltage applied to an analog input pin, and the eight tap signals are buffered to digital outputs. It requires external DC power for control and an oscilloscope for monitoring. Silicon tests show it works, achieving frequencies from 33 kHz to 2.8 MHz depending on bias current, with measured phase relationships among the taps.

This design generates a Mandelbrot set image and outputs it via a VGA driver, using an external RP2040 to emulate a framebuffer. It includes a serial interface for configuration and control, and the VGA output follows the Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD for display and an RP2040 for framebuffer emulation. The documentation is brief and lacks details on the serial protocol and exact operation, but the core function is clear.

This is a 16-bit CPU based on the HACK architecture, featuring an ALU, three registers (A, D, PC), and two SPI modules for memory and debug communication. It uses SPI to fetch instructions and data from an external SPI RAM, and a separate SPI debug interface allows reading internal registers. The design requires an external SPI RAM (e.g., 23XX512) and a microcontroller with SPI for debugging. It is notable for fitting a CPU into a single tile and using serial memory access due to pin limitations.

This is a demoscene project that displays a bouncing capsule with background and text on a VGA output, accompanied by PDM audio. It includes input switches to pause, reset, mute, hide elements, lock colors, and disable re-orientation. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD (or compatible) for output. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition and runs at 25 MHz.

This analog design implements a voltage divider using precision resistors that meander through geometric shapes to output a voltage of approximately π volts from a 3.3 V supply. The output is a single analog pin, and the design is tested by measuring the voltage with a multimeter. Silicon tests show an output of about 3.16 V, which is close to π when accounting for the actual supply voltage. The project is notable for its creative use of resistor geometry to achieve a mathematical constant.

This design implements several I2C peripherals: an FNV-1a 32-bit hash calculator, a leading zero counter (LZC), and two constant byte generators (0x55 and 0xAA). It demonstrates address decoding and I2C read/write operations, with each peripheral accessible via specific addresses. The design requires an I2C master device for testing, and Arduino test code is provided. It is a compact example of I2C peripheral integration.

This design converts I2S audio input to PWM output, with support for up to eight PDM microphones and beamforming via delay selection. It outputs PCM data for each microphone and a beamformed PCM output. The documentation is extremely sparse, using placeholder text like 'cool stuff', so the exact functionality and usage are unclear. External hardware needed includes PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver.

This is a 4-bit vector multiplication engine that multiplies two vectors of up to 32 elements and accumulates the result into an 8-bit output. It is programmed via a register interface using read/write opcodes and a run command, and it operates in two clock cycles. The design is intended to be controlled by an RP2040 and requires no other external hardware. Silicon tests show it works, though timing adjustments were needed.

This design displays a bouncing sprite with multiple background options on a VGA output, with sprite ROM, background control registers, and audio ROM configured via SPI. It requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and an audio PMOD for sound output. The design is controlled by SPI to set the background, sprite image, and sound effects. It is a hardware sprite engine suitable for simple games or demos.
